name: Milwaukee brace

image.caption: Milwaukee brace - with neck ring and mandible pad

lead: The Milwaukee brace is a rigid spinal orthosis that runs from the pelvis to the base of the skull. It is prescribed for growing children and teens with scoliosis or Scheuermann kyphosis, with the aim of holding the spine in a better position so the curve does not progress. A straighter spine means more even shoulders, a more balanced torso and a more upright posture.

It works through pads that press on the apex of the curve, a pelvic girdle that anchors the system, and a neck ring that keeps the head centred. Published series report that bracing changes the natural history of many curves, though results depend on curve type and on how many hours a day the brace is actually worn.

paras: The brace is custom fitted by an orthotist after X-rays. Historically it was worn around 23 hours a day until skeletal maturity, with periodic adjustments for growth; part-time protocols combined with physical therapy have also been reported. Newer, lower-profile braces are now more common for many curves.

Reported drawbacks include bulk and visibility, skin pressure, effects on quality of life and self-image, and variable compliance. Early versions with a chin-and-skull support were linked to effects on jaw and tooth development, which led to a redesigned throat-mold neck ring. Prolonged X-ray monitoring is part of treatment.

angle.text: For a growing person with a spinal curve, the brace is a medical way to keep the back straighter through puberty. A straighter spine supports a more symmetrical torso and a taller, more upright stance.

lead: The Milwaukee brace, also called a cervico-thoraco-lumbo-sacral orthosis (CTLSO), is a full-torso back brace used mainly to treat spinal curvature in growing children and adolescents [1]. By holding the spine in a corrected position during growth, it aims to prevent a curve from worsening, which in turn influences posture, shoulder and waist symmetry and overall torso appearance.

It was developed in the 1940s by orthopaedic surgeon Walter Blount, initially to support polio patients after spinal fusion, and was later applied to adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, with results published in 1956 [1]. It consists of a pelvic girdle, two posterior and one anterior upright bar, a neck ring with a throat mould and occipital pads, and adjustable pads that press on the curve [1].

Research includes large case series, a Scoliosis Research Society meta-analysis of non-operative treatments and, more recently, randomized trials of bracing in general. Reviews describe the Milwaukee brace as a historical standard that is still used for certain high thoracic curves and kyphosis [2][3].
infobox: Pelvic girdle, three uprights, neck ring, pads
About 23 hours a day until skeletal maturity [1]

paras: The brace is often custom moulded to the torso, though some are assembled from prefabricated parts. A leather or plastic pelvic girdle supports two posterior bars and one anterior bar that rise to a neck ring fitted with a throat mould and two occipital pads. Lateral pads strapped to the bars are adjusted to press on the curve [1].
Early versions used a mandibular-occipital support. Orthodontic studies in the 1970s examined its effects on the growing jaw, and the design was modified [4][5].

Blount first developed the brace in the 1940s for polio patients recovering from posterior spinal fusion and later used it for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, publishing results in 1956 [1]. A 1958 paper described how the brace was made [6]. It became widely used because casting was the main non-surgical alternative and the brace could be removed [1].
Reviews of North American bracing history place the Milwaukee brace alongside later designs such as the Wilmington, Boston, Charleston, Providence and SpineCor braces [7].

It is indicated mainly for growing adolescents with advancing curves of roughly 25 to 40 degrees, and occasionally adults with a collapsing deformity [1]. The usual historic protocol was about 23 hours a day until skeletal maturity [1]. A review of the brace's current role reported that even patients with other braces often wore them only about 60 percent of the prescribed time, and that part-time Milwaukee use combined with physical therapy gave better results than the natural history [2].

A review of 1,020 patients treated between 1954 and 1979 compared outcomes with a group of untreated patients to assess whether the brace altered the natural history of the disease [8]. An earlier series of 133 patients reported outcomes in thoracic and lumbar curves [9]. A 1974 review of 223 patients with Scheuermann kyphosis and postural roundback found that those who completed treatment improved their kyphosis by an average of about 40 percent [10].

A Scoliosis Research Society meta-analysis of 1,910 patients compared bracing, electrical stimulation and observation and reported weighted success proportions of 0.49 for observation and about 0.60 for bracing of eight hours daily, with higher figures for longer wear [3]. A 2008 review concluded that part-time Milwaukee wear could remain an option for thoracic or double curves [2]. The BrAIST randomized trial examined bracing in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis more broadly [11]. A controlled study examined the brace's effect on balance in hyperkyphotic adolescents [12], and a cross-sectional study of 102 adolescents examined how brace type affects quality of life [13].

Studies report effects on adolescents' self-perceived health and functioning, bulk, and variable compliance [2][13]. Repeated X-ray monitoring over a treatment programme adds radiation exposure, which was estimated in a 1979 study [14]. Jaw and dental effects of early neck-ring designs prompted redesign [4][5].
